extracted.intended_audience: researchers and authors conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses (health technology assessment / evidence synthesis teams)
extracted.subtask_short: assessing dissemination bias in systematic reviews
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for identifying, assessing and managing types of dissemination/publication biases (grey literature, language, citation, duplicate, place/country/indexing/media biases) when conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses in health care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grey literature bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Available evidence from good quality studies suggested that published studies tend to report a greater treatment effect compared with a more complete set of data from published and unpublished studies, but that for individual reviews the effects may not always be in this direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies using an unbiased sample of multiple meta-analyses provide the most valid evidence on grey literature bias. The impact of grey literature in meta-analysis is usually small, although occasionally data from grey literature may have important clinical implications. A case-by-case approach is required to decide whether grey literature should be comprehensively searched and included in systematic reviews. The inclusion of grey literature may sometimes introduce bias, as will exclusion of grey literature in other cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conference abstracts and unpublished data
rubrics_metrics.description: The most commonly included unpublished data used in reviews are conference abstracts, but there are difficulties in using data from abstracts as they provide limited information, may be on partial datasets and may be misleading when compared with later full publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat data from abstracts cautiously because of limited reporting, partial datasets and potential for discrepancy with full publications. Consider verification or seeking full data where possible before inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language bias (including searching non-English studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many prestigious international scientific journals are published in English… The best way to ensure that a review does not contain language bias is to search for and include relevant non-English language studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact of excluding non-English studies is heterogeneous: exclusion often reduces precision and may or may not bias effect estimates; it may substantially alter meta-analyses in areas such as complementary medicine. Decide whether to include non-English studies on a case-by-case basis, balancing potential bias against searching/translation cost-effectiveness (which is unclear). When possible include non-English studies and assess changes by subsequently excluding them to gauge impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of studies by language is not a reason for automatic exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies published in languages other than English cannot be generally excluded for the reason of study quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical comparisons found only minor or inconsistent differences in methodological quality between English and non-English trials; therefore language alone should not determine exclusion. Assess study quality directly rather than using language as a proxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation bias occurs when the probability that a study will be cited is associated with the study result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evidence indicates that studies with positive or significant results are on average associated with a higher frequency of citation. Non-systematic narrative reviews are particularly vulnerable to biased citation, which can lead to misleading conclusions. When synthesising evidence, check for selective citation patterns and prioritise systematic, comprehensive identification of studies rather than relying on cited literature alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate (multiple) publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicate, redundant, repetitive or multiple publications are defined as submission of similar manuscripts to more than one journal or the republication of the same data in two or more journals. Duplicate publication can be classified as ‘overt’ or ‘covert’. Covert duplicate publication is when the same data are published in different places or at different times without adequate reference to a previous or parallel publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covert duplicate publication may introduce bias into systematic reviews by including the same data more than once and magnifying weights. Detecting duplicates is difficult (changing authorship, different patient numbers, partial reporting). Use methods to detect duplicates (e.g., text-similarity tools, careful cross-referencing) and classify duplicates as covert/non-covert; exclude or account for duplicated data in meta-analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Place of publication bias occurs when, for reasons of editorial policy or readers’ preference, one journal is more enthusiastic towards publishing articles about a given hypothesis than other journals; trials with significant results tend to be published in prominent journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that significant trials are more likely to appear in high-impact journals; this can skew perception of evidence if searches or reliance focus on prominent journals. Ensure comprehensive searches across journals of varying impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Variable results from studies on the same topic between different countries may reflect publication bias; some countries (e.g., China, Taiwan, Japan, USSR/Russia in examples) have reported unusually high proportions of positive results in certain fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search beyond MEDLINE and western databases to capture country-specific literature; be cautious interpreting large bodies of non-indexed literature because they may exhibit high levels of publication bias. Also note underrepresentation of research from developing countries can bias the research agenda and evidence base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Database indexing bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Database indexing bias occurs when there is biased indexing of published studies in literature databases, so that the results of indexed studies are systematically different from those of non-indexed studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that major literature databases over-represent western-developed-country journals. Design search strategies that include multiple databases and regional sources to reduce indexing bias; consider handsearching and non-indexed sources where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media attention bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Media attention bias occurs when studies with striking results are more likely to be covered by newspapers, radio and television news, and the overly optimistic portrayal of findings affects public perception and policy discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate media prominence with scientific validity. Be aware that media reports often omit basic study facts and may preferentially report positive results; when using media-reported research, trace back to the original studies and assess validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the available evidence on dissemination biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical studies on publication and related biases have focused mainly on certain areas of research such as clinical trials of health-care interventions. There is only very limited evidence on publication bias in many other research fields including basic research and observational studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret empirical findings with caution because many studies are heterogeneous, based on case reports, and vulnerable to confounding and selective reporting. Prefer less selective cohorts (e.g., registered protocols) for stronger evidence on biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome reporting bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Recently published studies have provided convincing evidence that outcome reporting bias exists and is likely to have important effects on pooled summary data within systematic reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome reporting bias appears to affect harm and subjectively assessed outcomes more than efficacy and objectively assessed outcomes. Systematic reviewers should compare protocols/registrations with published reports to detect selective outcome reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of inclusion/exclusion decisions on meta-analysis estimates and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding non-English-language studies reduced the precision of the estimate of effect. Inclusion or exclusion of non-English-language studies or duplicates can change treatment effect estimates and confidence intervals in individual meta-analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sensitivity of meta-analytic results to inclusion/exclusion of grey literature, non-English studies, duplicates, and non-indexed studies (e.g., perform analyses with and without these studies) because direction and magnitude of change are unpredictable and heterogeneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended case-by-case approach to handling dissemination biases
rubrics_metrics.description: A case-by-case approach is required to gauge the possible impact of publication and related biases and to decide appropriate measures to deal with these biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each review, weigh the likelihood and potential direction of bias against resources required (searching, translation). Where feasible, include broader searches (grey literature, non-English, registries), then test the impact by excluding subsets; document decisions and rationale transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification tools and practical challenges for duplicate detection
rubrics_metrics.description: A database of duplicate publication and potential plagiarism (Déjà vu) has been developed by using a text similarity algorithm to identify extremely similar references from MEDLINE. However, multiple publications are often difficult to detect because the first author and the number of authors cited often differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use automated tools (text-similarity algorithms, duplicate-detection databases) in combination with manual checks (author lists, sample sizes, dates, methods) to identify potential duplicates. Be alert to inconsistent reporting across publications (different patient numbers, different authorship) that may signal covert duplication.
